utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If the witness could be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Please be seated. I would remind you of the affirmation you took at the beginning of your evidence which still applies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, can you understand me okay?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I believe I told you this yesterday, but again, if at any time you don't understand one of my questions please let me know and I'll try to put it in a better way. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. The first thing I would like to do is to go over a couple of things you told us yesterday to make sure that we have a clear record.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we go briefly into private session for the first one of these points, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, yesterday I asked you some questions about when you were taken off of the bus, and you told us that -- first, do you remember those questions?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If someone were to remind me, I would remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. To help you recall, you told us that there were a few other Serbs on the bus besides you and your family. And I believe you told us that you and your son and the men named Genov and Cuk were asked by a soldier to leave the bus. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And I simply forgot to ask you: Were there any Serbs on the bus who were not asked off?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on when I met up with my wife, I heard about that. There was some commotion with my wife, so then the man who was asking for IDs, checking documents, did not go all the way to the end of the bus but he stopped where my wife was because of all the commotion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll move on to another question. You remember that yesterday I asked you a number of questions about when you first arrived at this place where you were held. And I don't mean the school building, but the place that you described as a house on a farm. Do you remember that generally?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And I'll read you the specific passage that I'd like to focus on. My question was: "What happened when you arrived at your destination?"

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is page 1305 of the corrected transcript. I believe it's page 68 on the other version.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me repeat that. My question to you was: "What happened when you arrived at your destination?" And you answered: "They entered the yard then. There was a big gate there. We stood in front of the door of a house and they took the two of them in and they took the two of us in, Ivan and me that is." And I asked you: "Did they remove your blindfold?" You said: "Yes, it was nighttime. You couldn't see anything in the yard."

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: At this time I would ask the assistance of Mr. Younis. Your Honours, with your permission, if the witness could be given a copy of what was marked yesterday as P77 for identification. This was a prior statement of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: On what basis would the witness be looking at that at this point?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I just wanted to point out an inconsistency between what he said yesterday and what's in the statement and try to see if he could in fact remember how it happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The statement is not in evidence. His evidence yesterday stands as the evidence. Unless it is ventured in some cross-examination, we will not get to explore that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Sorry. It's not here a question of whether his evidence is consistent with all his previous statements. You realise that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I do, of course. I'm just trying to make things as clear as I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm grateful, but I'm afraid that there are some lingerings of the common law of evidence that we must stick to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Bakrac, I'll move on to a new question. You also told us yesterday that at some point you were taken to a basement. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After that building, we were taken to the basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me again refer to the specific passage that I'm interested in right now. My question was: "You say that they transferred you to another room. Describe how that happened, please." And you said: "I cannot give you the exact details, but at any rate after the incident with the knife, soon after that, we all went to the basement. First the two of them, and then they wondered what they'd do with us and then they said we should be taken to the basement, too." Then I asked you: "Do you remember who should be taken to the basement, too?" And your answer was: "I don't know who said that. At any rate, I do know that it had been said." Mr. Bakrac, do you think it would refresh your recollection if you could look at the statement you made on the 2nd of August, 1998?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That would be an improper use for the notion of refreshing recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, my remark is somewhat different. At the commencement of this witness's evidence yesterday, he was asked by my learned friend if he had had an opportunity, in addition to making the statement and in addition to the proofing system that the Prosecution engages in, to read the statement which my friend now talks about. He said he had. And he had accordingly already used that document as a memory-refreshing document outside the court. It is hardly fair, in my submission, or appropriate to ask him in effect to crib off that statement now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If I could respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I would be grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I asked him if he could remember who said that he should be taken to the basement. He said, "I don't know who said that." Perhaps I could ask him again if he remembers, or if he doesn't remember. And if he doesn't remember, it seems that I should be allowed to refresh his recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's where our understanding may differ, I'm afraid, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'll absolutely obviously go with your understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You can ask the first question, but there's not point in it if you're not going to get past the second one.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I don't know if I've achieved any clarification of yesterday, but I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: On some other matters, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, I'd now like to go back to where you left off yesterday. You had just described to us how you and the other prisoners were arranged in the basement. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Now, with the assistance of Mr. Younis and the Sanction system, I'd like to show a part of Prosecution Exhibit P5, which is the 360 presentation. Mr. Bakrac, do you recognise the place that you see on your screen?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Is this the basement where you were taken?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If Mr. Younis could take us inside that room.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, here now, do you recognise what's on the screen now?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not with these things, but it is the basement. It looked different when it was empty and when there were only people there. There were some shelves on the wall, and I remember one night I slept below that shelf. My head was underneath that shelf.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Perhaps I could ask Mr. Younis to give us another view.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you recognise that image as well, sir?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's what it looked like. But as I said, these things weren't in there then.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You told us that one night you slept below a shelf, that your head was underneath the shelf. Can you tell us based on what you see in front of you which shelf that was?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question. Could you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Of course. It was not a very good question; it wasn't very clear. Looking at the image if in front of you, can you describe to us which one of those shelves you slept under.

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, underneath that shelf on the right-hand side, and one night on the shelf itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. I think we're done with Sanction for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for the record, that last image I'm Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. told by Mr. Younis is the same as in the locations booklet and bears the ERN U0083678, just for the future reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, how long were you and your son held in that basement?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think two or three days and two or three nights. Not longer than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'd like you to describe that basement. And first I'll ask you: What was the floor made of, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first it was covered with straw and hay. I could not say with any degree of certainty whether there was any concrete, too, but possibly there was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you have space in the basement to stretch out in?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There wasn't enough space for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Was there a toilet in the basement?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: How did you relieve yourselves?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a can by the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Were you allowed outside of this basement, sir?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Was the door guarded?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Somebody was there all the time. People like guards and -- it wasn't that there was someone there all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you remember any of those guards in particular?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember when in the morning a man came and walked in and brought a pack of cigarettes to every one of the people there who smoked and breakfast, too -- no, actually, there wasn't any breakfast. That was the first meeting with the guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Who was it that brought you food and cigarettes?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the men there, they called him Shala. I remember that. I had a lot of contact with him later.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: How old was Shala?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Perhaps 45, 50. I can't say anything for sure. He was an older person, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you remember how tall he was?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Perhaps around my height, shorter, taller, I don't know. Something like that, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Can you describe his face?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had a cap and he had a black moustache.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What colour was his hair?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was dark. Sort of darker hair.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Other than the cap that he wore, do you remember how he was dressed?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What was Shala's role in the camp?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that question could be phrased somewhat differently. I think it's somewhat suggestive. Perhaps I'm being a bit precipitous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think you may be at this point. You're ahead of me by a long shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I'll sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Please answer the question if you can, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His role was probably to be there as a kind of guard. He communicated with us who were detained there. He brought us food and cigarettes. And that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: How did Shala treat you and your son?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nicely. We didn't have any contacts in the basement, no special contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You say you didn't have any special contacts. Could you explain what you mean, please.

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were in the basement and no one asked us a thing. The only thing they did was take off our gold chains, the ones we wore around our necks. It happened one night; I don't know who did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you have contacts with Shala after you left the basement?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. We spoke just formally, nothing specific; when we'd see each other, when he'd come to see us, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Maybe I can ask it more clearly. How often did you see Shala approximately?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We saw him whenever he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And how often was that?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They changed, these people who were there as a kind of guards. There were two other men besides him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I want to ask this in a non-leading way, so perhaps you can guide me if I've gone astray.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, did you see Shala once a day? Once a week? Can you help us on the frequency with which you saw him.

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While we were in the basement, we didn't see him. When they transferred us to the room in the main building, then we would see him. Sometimes it would happen a few times a day, of course, when he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. You say you spoke just formally with Shala. Did you look directly at him when you spoke with him?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And how far away from him were you when you spoke with him?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way you normally talk to a person, not from far away. We were in the same room.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to ask you: While you were in the basement, did any of the detainees tell you whether they had been beaten or not?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They said that they had not been beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Was anyone beaten while you were in the basement?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Genov was taken out and then brought back half an hour or an hour later and he would be beaten up.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: How many times did this happen?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every day. It seems to me that it would be once, and I remember that at one point -- one night they took him out twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What time of day did they take Genov out to be beaten up?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once it was during the day and all the other cases happened at night.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you ever see the people who came to take out Genov?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was night. I remember that they had hoods on their heads, and even if they had not had hoods it would have been impossible for us to see their faces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What condition was Genov in when he returned to the basement after these beatings?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many times he was semi-conscious. He had been beaten up pretty badly. One time he was unconscious.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you try to help Genov?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had a handkerchief. I wet it with some water. And Ivan and myself put it on him, on his -- the kidney area, and on his chest as a kind of poultice or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Was Genov able to use the bucket to relieve himself?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was unable to relieve himself. I know that once we brought the bucket to him to relieve himself. He was unable to go himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did Genov ever speak to you about his condition or ask you for help?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One night he asked me first -- or I don't remember. Maybe it was Ivan first. He asked us to strangle him because he was unable to go on. I couldn't do that; Ivan couldn't do that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: While you were in the basement, other than the people there with you, did you ever see any other people who appeared to be prisoners?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't see anyone from the basement. In fact, we only saw some people passing by. We didn't dare approach the window but we could see people passing by.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: When you say "passing by," could you tell where they were going or where they were coming from?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't see them. In fact, we heard their footsteps. And then we would hear footsteps again, maybe half an hour later, of people coming back.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, while you were held in the basement were you ever informed of why you were being held?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nobody told us why. One day the Krstic brothers told us that we would be released, that there was no reason for us to fear, that Ivan and I would be released.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: But from the soldiers, did any one of them ever tell you that you were charged with an offence?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, you said that you were in the basement for approximately two or three days or two days and two nights. Did you eventually leave the basement?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at one point. I think it was on the third day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you and Ivan leave the basement at the same time?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. First a gentleman came for Ivan and said that he should get out. He went out, the door closed. I was very upset. I started crying, and the others tried to calm me down, to say not to worry, that nothing would happen. But I am a father.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Can you describe the person who came for Ivan and said that he should get out?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a man who was taller than I am. He wore a uniform, a camouflage uniform, a neat uniform. He had a small beard and an officer's satchel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you remember about how old he was?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps in his 30s, 30, 35. He was younger than I am, if my memory serves me right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did this commander tell you anything about himself, about his background or his education?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, my friend of course knows the objection that's coming. I think what he can say is: Did that person say anything to you at all? But there's no need obviously to suggest a particular subject of conversation when that has not been even touched upon by the witness. If it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm not inclined to agree, Mr. Khan. Directing the witness's attention to a particular subject and asking whether that was spoken about is not suggesting what that might be the content of any conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: So be it, I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I have a slightly different observation, Your Honour, which is that he is leading the witnesses in identifying this particular individual as having a particular role and a particular status, one which this particular witness has not identified before the question asked. And that is specifically of -- and by mentioning it of course I'm going to --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Perhaps I can help. I see the problem. That was a mistake of mine. I'll rephrase the question in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: That's very kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, this person that you've just described, did he tell you anything about himself, about his background or his education?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems to me that he didn't say anything in the basement, but I did have another encounter with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: During that other encounter did he tell you anything about himself, his background or his education?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He merely said that he was a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, could you tell what this person's position was at the camp?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know what his position was, his function. But I know that Albanians are very obedient people and he was obeyed by the others. So I assume that he had a superior position because they do respect superiors. I used to be a manager and I know how the Albanians treated me, and that is what led me to conclude that he had a superior position.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. You said he was obeyed by the others. Which others do you mean?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant the people who were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you mean the other people -- the Albanians in the basement with you or someone else?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm referring to the people who were there: soldiers, guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before you move on I must apologise to you, Mr. Khan. I had missed the opening two words of what had been the question Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that was concerning you and the reference to commander. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, you were describing how Ivan had been told that he needed to get out of the basement and your reaction. Please tell us what happened next.

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Soon after one of the soldiers came. I don't remember who it was. He came to pick me up. And I went to the main building on the ground floor. The room where Ivan and this gentleman sat. Ivan was drinking tea. They were chit-chatting. I walked in and he told me that Ivan would no longer have to stay in the basement, in the stink that was there, that it was no place for him. And I don't remember all the other things that he said. I remember those particular words. Soon after that I was taken back to the basement. I took it really hard. I'm a very emotional person. It wasn't easy for me to leave my son there. I went to the basement, and perhaps half an hour, an hour -- half an hour later the door opened once again and Mr. Shala called me out. I went out and saw Ivan sitting on the grass in the yard a bit further up the well, because there was a well there. I joined him and I also sat down. And I felt much, much easier. We didn't sit there for a long time. I heard the sound of a car engine. Mr. Shala took us to the first floor upstairs in the building, in the main building. And until the moment of our release, we remained there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me stop you there for a moment and ask Mr. Younis, again with the Sanction, to put Prosecution Exhibit P5 up. It's the 360 presentation. Mr. Bakrac, there will be an image on your screen now. Do you recognise that place?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And when you say "the first floor," "upstairs in the main building," which building do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Perhaps Mr. Younis could pan around.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the building. If you could go back a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If Mr. Younis could go back a bit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps for the record again, in the locations booklet this is the building which bears the ERN U0083669. Perhaps Mr. Younis can take us into the upstairs of that building. And if he can pan around.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'll ask you, Mr. Bakrac, to watch this for a moment. Mr. Bakrac, do you recognise this place?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is the room where Ivan and I were.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did that room look any differently at the time you were there than it does in the images you have seen?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, mostly it looked like that. The shelf with the TV was there. The aerial and the foam mattresses were on the floor. That was some kind of a room for ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Please continue. I'm sorry to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The foam mattresses were lined up there. It was some kind of a room for rest. And that's where they kept some other people, not just us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That was my next question. Was anyone else in this room when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sure that there were two of them. I'm not sure whether there was a third man, too. But two I'm sure were there when we arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'll ask Mr. Younis to take the Sanction off. We're done with that for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, what can you describe about these two men who were there when you arrived? What can you tell me about them?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two young Albanian men. They were there also in some kind of detention. We spoke to them, so I know what it was all about. They also told us that we should not be afraid, that we would be released. They were there undergoing some kind of a check-up. I don't know if they had any connections with the Serb side. That's what they were checking up, because they wanted to join the Kosovo army. One of them was called "Gzim," I know that for sure. I don't know which one of them it was. One of them had worked in Switzerland and he told me that he had been working there for years and giving them money for the cause and now he had to sit there, wait in detention. The other one was there slightly longer than the first one. He was also undergoing some checks, background checks, because of suspicion that he had been collaborating with Serbs. That's what they told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: How many days were you held in this room, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were there in this room for five days, until the day when we were released.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you ever go back to the room on the ground floor, the first one that you were taken to when you arrived at the farm?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On one occasion we were called to go down there. We had tea. We sat there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did anything else happen besides having tea?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was an unpleasant situation for me and for my son. We had to watch as other men were beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I know it's unpleasant, but I'm going to ask you to describe that occasion for the Trial Chamber. First, do you remember how many men were there being beaten?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They brought four or five of them. I don't know the exact number, but it wasn't more than five. They lined them up and started beating them. They would beat every one of them for five or ten minutes, slapping them, kicking them, hitting them on their legs. One of them was unable to stand at all. At any rate, they were beaten up.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of the soldiers who participated in the beating?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The same man that beat Genov beat these people. I'm referring to the first day when we arrived there, in that facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Was this person armed now on this occasion that you're describing right now?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had a pistol.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did he do anything with that pistol?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that. When they stopped beating them he handed the pistol to one of these men and he told him to kill the others. The man lifted the pistol up and put him next to a person's forehead. They were crying, begging for mercy. Then this first man took the pistol, put it next to the other man's forehead and fired it, but it was empty. I think it was some kind of psychological torture.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: While you and your son were watching this, were you sitting alone?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were -- there was Ivan, myself, and the man -- the gentleman who had come to get Ivan out of the basement, the man I referred to as the superior, as the commander. At one point he told me that these were traitors to their people. He asked me, What do you do with your traitors? I merely said, Treason is treason. That's what I said. I don't know at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did this superior tell you anything else on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but before that he had said that he was a lawyer. So he did say some things. But I don't really remember exactly. Apart from this thing that he asked me, What do you do with your traitors?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: How long did this incident last?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not long. Half an hour, 45 minutes, an hour at the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And what happened when it was over? Where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were taken back to the room upstairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, did you ever see Stamen Genov again after you were taken upstairs?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never saw Genov or Cuk or any other person from there again.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm not asking if you spoke with him, but did you ever learn anything more about Genov while you were still at this farm?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One day we did learn --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm sorry. I do recall the events but I can't remember the exact order in which they took place, whether it was yesterday or the day before, but I do remember the event itself. Please do take that into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Please describe this event where you learned more about Genov.

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were in the room upstairs and were using the toilet that was also used by the others. One day they told us not to use the toilet anymore but to use the one at the bottom of the yard because the masters of the house were here now and the toilet was for their use. So Ivan one day went to the toilet and he asked, What happened with the sergeant? The people standing at the window of the basement told him that they had been told that he had been released. That was the only thing that we had heard about Genov.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: While you were in the upstairs, were you ever asked to give a statement?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were told that we would have to give a statement before being released about how we fared in the camp, how we were treated. In general, we were supposed to write down everything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Who told you this, that you were going to have to give this statement?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were told by this gentleman, the commander. That's what I call him. I don't know whether he was one or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Is this the same person that had come to take Ivan out of the basement? Is that who you mean?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the man. I had a little chat with him there. I felt a bit freer and I asked him something about their military, whether they had any kind of international recognition, everything that came to my mind. He told me that they did not have international recognition but they were working on it. That was the first time I asked him a direct question, whether we would be released or not. And he said, Yes, we only have to find a way to transfer you and also find a place to transfer you to. I felt much better after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Were you told that you would give a written statement or a spoken statement? What kind of statement were you going to have to give?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They told us that we should make a written statement about everything that had happened to us, both Ivan and myself, and that we would probably have to repeat all that before a camera. But first we had to write everything down so they see what our statements would be like, to see what we had to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And did they review the statement that you wrote?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The day after they brought me a piece of paper and a pencil, and then they had a look at the statements. They were happy with it, with my statement. And then they said that I would have to repeat the same thing before a camera, that I would be taped and that Ivan would be taped, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And did that eventually happen?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did. It was in the early evening -- it was in the early evening. We were sitting in the room. Two gunshots were heard; Ivan and I remember that. Then these people came, this commander, Shala. There must have been about seven or eight of them. It was the first time I saw most of them there. There was one man among them who was well-built. He had a pistol in his hand. First he talked to us about a greater Albania, that it was theirs, what were we doing there; We were taking jobs away from Albanians, that our children went to school and that their children did not go to school. That's what everybody told us, whoever we talked to. At one moment he said, I can kill your son. And that shocked me. I started shaking and I probably had a nervous breakdown then. And he said, Ah, you're shaking and our people don't have a chance to shake before your people. He was speaking in Serbian but not pure Serbian. Then he turned to Shala and asked him to clean his pistol for him. It was our understanding then that Genov had been killed; we assumed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Why did you assume then that Genov had been killed?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I put the puzzle together, that they told Ivan that he had been released and then the gunshots rang out and then no one heard of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you then make your video statement that they'd said you'd have to make?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was sitting in a chair. They were around us, all these men. One man placed a video camera on a tripod. He was a big man in uniform; they all wore uniforms. There was also a very nice gentleman there, very tidy, an elderly gentleman, rather short, but a very well-groomed person. I started talking, saying that they did not Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. mistreat us, that they did not beat us, that they were a regular army, that they had their duties. I went on talking but with a bit of nervousness and a bit of fear, which was noticeable. So I had to repeat it but without any fear. I repeated my statement before the camera. They were pleased with my statement. I was not allowed to mention the basement, but I was mainly supposed to talk about what happened to us, how we were treated, and what they did to us. I said all of that, what did they do to us? Nothing. That we had cigarettes, that we had water, that we had food. At that moment I would have said anything to set us free.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What about your son, Ivan, did he also give a statement?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he gave a statement, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And do you remember what he said?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He repeated what I had said, because we were sitting next to each other so he heard it. He also mentioned that he had played chess with Shala, which was true.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did any of these soldiers tell you anything about why you were being held or how long you would be held?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They just said that we would be there until - how should I put this? - they find the right place and time to get in touch with the UNHCR and the International Red Cross, who were supposed to take care of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: After giving these statements, did you remain in the upstairs?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What else, if anything, happened in your last days there? Do you remember speaking to anyone?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked to this commander, to -- yes, when I asked him whether we would be set free, I asked him whether he could phone my wife and tell her that we were alive and well. He had a mobile telephone. He said that he could not do that from a mobile phone but that he could do it. I gave him my mother-in-law's telephone number. And I thought that perhaps he would call because I did not see any reason why he wouldn't do this for me if he said he could. And he really did it. He called my wife's mother and said that Vojko and Ivan were alive and we would be released. The following day he did tell me that he had called.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Please tell the Trial Chamber what happened on your last day at this farm.

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last day they came to get us, if that's what you're referring to. We heard a door squeaking at one point and a car came into the yard. Ivan and I were standing there, or rather I looked through the window and I saw a Jeep and a lot of soldiers wearing uniforms. They came upstairs and this nice gentleman, who I described a few minutes ago that he was an elderly man but very well-groomed, he said to me the previous day that we would be released. He gave me his word of honour, their Albanian word of honour, and I believed him. And that indeed came true. He said to me, See, the moment has come for you to go home. I asked for my gold chain and the ring my wife had given to me as a gift. They had forgotten about that, so they went to get it. They returned perhaps half an hour later. They didn't bring my documents, though, but I did need my refugee ID. However, they said that they couldn't find it. I said that they put everything in Genov's wallet in the school. When we were first brought to the school they picked up all the documents and put them all into Genov's wallet. He came back and said, You're right, it was there. He brought us our things. We put on our shoes that had been on the stairs and we went to the Jeep. We said goodbye to Shala and left.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: The fact that your documents had been in Genov's wallet where you said they were, did that suggest anything to you about Genov's fate?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did know, because they said that whoever was released would receive all of his things.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Could you please explain that a little more.

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About what? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You said that: "Whoever was released would receive all of his things," but what did that tell you about Genov? I don't understand. Could you please explain it.

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since Genov's wallet was there, that meant that it had not been returned to him. So that confirmed my suspicion that he had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You said you said goodbye to Shala and left. Please explain what happened then.

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We got into the Jeep. There were two men sitting in front. Now, was there someone behind us? I can't remember that. They blindfolded us and we set off. It was still daytime. We took the macadam road. We probably took a road that went all the way around; it was not an asphalt road. We drove on for about 15 or 20 minutes, and then we turned abruptly at a 90-degree angle. That's where they took off our blindfolds. I don't know how long we drove along the asphalt road, but then we came to a settlement where many people lived. It was Malisevo. I saw a lot of people at the gasoline station and shops, so I assumed that it was Malisevo. We came to a place where we stopped. I had already noticed two white Jeeps of the Red Cross about 200 metres away from us. A man was standing there. He had a scar on his face; I remember that, but I don't remember which side. He said that we should stand there and wait for a while. They went up to these people from the Red Cross. These were two women, actually. They had a Jeep each. They drove a Jeep each. Then they spent some time at a cafe that was there, perhaps 15 or 20 minutes, and then they went back to their Jeeps and then they set out. First there was a car, then the two Jeeps, and then us, and then somebody else behind us. So we left that town or that settlement. After a while, I don't know how much time had gone by, everybody stopped. We had to get out of the Jeep. The two women got out, too, or girls, I don't know. The women or girls from the Red Cross, they didn't speak Serbian or Albanian. They had a gentleman who interpreted both Serbian and Albanian for them. He was probably interpreting into English because they were English. We got off the Jeep and we were supposed to take off our shirts so that they could see that we had not been injured, so they could see that we didn't have any scars, and indeed we didn't have any scars, so we showed them that. And then we got into the International Red Cross Jeep. Ivan and I were inside, still trembling, not believing all of this. And we set out. We drove for a while and then we stopped again. There was a kind of checkpoint there, barricades, military men, and that's where the man with a scar said that these two Jeeps had to pass through. We saw that the person at the checkpoint was in two minds, wondering why he had to let us go. I was in the car wondering what they were saying, but there was a discussion between him and the man with a scar. We were a bit afraid then, but after a minute or two it was over. We continued our journey to Pristina. These women drove us to Pristina. One was in front and we were in the back -- in the Jeep. That's how we reached Pristina, the International Red Cross. They met us there, these people from this international body, and a lady. If I remember correctly her name was Ruzica Simic. That was the lady who had sent us to Djakovica. She was a secretary for refugees for Kosovo. We were taken to her house for a day or two. I can't remember exactly for how long. She gave us clothing so that we could change, take a bath, get some rest. And that's how things went. That's how Ivan and I were released from that camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, what was your reaction when you realised that you were free?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just cried. I couldn't stop crying. No one could stop me. The following month or month and a half, whenever I would meet someone I knew I would burst into tears. I couldn't even talk. I went to see a psychiatrist at the hospital for refugees and I went there every day for two or three weeks. Until the present day when I speak to someone on the telephone, I can't talk. I simply burst into tears if it's a person I like.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Why do you think that you and your son were kidnapped?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- well, it's not that I think. We were not of Albanian ethnicity. In my son's documents and in my documents it doesn't say that we are Serbs at all. In my documents it says that I was born in Brezice and in Ivan's documents that he was born in Zagreb, but it's the name and surname.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Why do you think you were released?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- I think that we were mistakenly taken off the bus, now that I look at all the facts. And my wife did a great thing. After we were taken off the bus, she stopped the bus at the first checkpoint and told everybody what had happened. She did not sleep, she did not eat. She went from one house to another, practically. She was on television, the Voice of America, CNN. She was all over the place. She told everybody what had happened, not only to me but also to the other two men, that we were kidnapped. At one moment while we were upstairs, a man came and he said to me, Your wife was on television yesterday. And then my Ivan said, Oh my God, Daddy. But the man said, Don't worry about what she said. They watched it over satellite TV. It was the Voice of America. All things considered, I think I was taken off the bus mistakenly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have any further questions at this time. You can tender the witness for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have a break now and it will be -- there's reason for the Chamber to have a slightly longer break than usual. We will resume at 10 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honours, my friends have asked me to go first --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I asked to go first.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: That's right. It was one or the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And you are content, Mr. Guy-Smith, because if you're not --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I am content. It's just I think it's so terribly important the record is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You may correctly go first, Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, I represent a man called Isak Musliu. I just have a few questions for you. You made a statement to the Organisation for Humanitarian Law on the 2nd of August, 1998. Do you recollect doing that?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And as Mr. Black established with you yesterday, you made a statement to this Tribunal in January of 2003.

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I want to ask you about an interview that you had, however, earlier than any of those dates, Mr. Bakrac. And that is an interview that you described yesterday as having had with the Serbian authorities. Do you remember telling us a bit about that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: The date on which this interview took place may, sir, have been the 7th of July of 1998. Now, I don't suppose for one moment you've kept these dates entirely clear in your mind, but can you help us? Could that be the correct date for this first interview with the Serbian authorities?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the date, but it was after my release.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we can work it this way, I think, together. You were taken from the bus in the last days of June, were you not?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the 29th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. Your best estimate in your statement to the ICTY investigators was that you were in the camp, as you've described it, for some seven or eight days. Do you remember saying that to them?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That would be it, up to ten days, not more than ten days.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And if you saw the Serbian authorities the day after your release that would take us, wouldn't it, by the calendar at least until about the 6th or 7th of July. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the date. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, it's gracious of you to apologise. You don't have to, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. because I have an advantage over you. I have a note of a meeting, an official note that has been disclosed to us by the Prosecution. It's signed by someone called Corporal Stankovic. Now, do you remember the names of anyone you saw the day after your release in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember, because I don't know anyone in Pristina apart from Ms. Ruzica Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Was it your own idea or was it at the suggestion of somebody else that you went to the office of the State Security Centre in Pristina the day after your release?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We were called to go there both by the military and by the state security service. The military was supposed to pick us up but we couldn't tell one from the other. They took us to the state security centre; they are the police. That's the police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes. Was the coordinator of that centre a man called David Gajic?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Did you receive a request delivered to you by a person or did you receive something in writing to go to the State Security Centre in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If my memory serves me right, I did not receive anything in writing. I think it was just a telephone conversation, a telephone call that we received either in the house of Ruzica Simic or at the Red Cross. I don't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Very well. When you went to the office of the state security centre, who else was with you, if anybody?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My son Ivan was with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And was he there during the entirety of the interview you had with the Serbian police?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I'll try not to repeat my questions. Did I understand your evidence to be a moment ago that you can't remember the name of anyone you saw there on the Serbian side, any of the officials. Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, let me just put two names to you to see if either or both of these ring any bells. And may I, sir, indicate that I am looking again at a Serbian document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Would it be possible to have an ERN number for reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes, of course it would. I have an EDT number, Mr. Black, if that will help which is 0188-5938 to 0188-5939.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: That, Mr. Bakrac, is a reference number on the top of a document that is called a criminal report. It's a criminal report that relates in part to your being taken from the bus. So that's what I have in front of me. Do you understand me? That report is signed by Dragan Jasevic and Momcilo Sparalevo. Do either of those names mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I've already mentioned Stankovic, whose name appears at the bottom of a note dated the 7th of July, a corporal Stankovic. There's only one other name on this other document that has -- the only reference number on it, for Mr. Black's benefit, 0188-5957 from a Major Petar, P-e-t-a-r. Does that name mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Can you recollect now, sir, how many Serbian police officers were present when you and Ivan, your son, were speaking with them in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Did they appear to be of equal rank or did one appear to be more senior than the other?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Were either or both of them in uniform?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, they were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Only a lawyer could ask such a ridiculous-sounding question as the next one, and I'm a lawyer so I'm going to ask it. Were any of them making notes, as far as you can remember? Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were taking notes with a pencil in some kind of a notepad.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Were you asked to read or sign these notes at the end of your meeting?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not read them and I cannot recall whether I signed them or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: By the time you were speaking with them, did they indicate to you that they knew that Genov had been taken from the same bus as you? Did they seem to know that?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Did they know -- did they seem to be aware that your wife had been speaking to Voice of America and CNN and that therefore your taking was in the public arena? Did they seem to know that?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was known to the public. I still have the press clippings to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I'm sure it's my fault, Mr. Bakrac, and I apologise to you. That wasn't quite the answer to the question I asked you. The question was: Did these interviewing Serbian officers, whatever they were, whoever they were, did they seem to know that your wife had been on television speaking about your taking?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It seems to me that they did not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: In due course, as we know, both in August of 1998, in other words the next month from this meeting, and then several years later to the ICTY in 2003, you were able to give, were you not, detailed accounts of your stay in this place in Lapusnik? We've had a lot of examples of the detailed evidence you've been able to give. Do you agree? You were able to give detailed accounts in due course of what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the first part of your question; I didn't quite understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: It was a bad question, it was overlong. In due course you were able to give a lot of detailed information about what happened to you. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Did you provide a lot of detailed information to these two Serbian officers at your meeting with them probably on the 7th of July, 1998? Can you recollect?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I told them about what had happened to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Were there any maps or plans out at this meeting, Mr. Bakrac? Did they produce any maps or plans for you to look at, anything like that?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Were you asked to draw any map or plan or sketch in relation to where you had been taken by them?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because I did not know where I had been taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: In anything either of these Serb officers said, did either of them seem to be aware of the existence of a place in Lapusnik where people were being held? Did they seem to know about it, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about that place. I learned after my release about Crnoljevo. That was the only place that I had learned about. And as for this other place, I didn't know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Again, sir, if I's my fault I apologise. I didn't ask you what you knew. I was asking you whether from their questions -- these two Serbian officers, 7th of July -- from what they were saying to you, did they seem to know anything about this place where you had been.

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Did they suggest to you the names of any KLA soldiers operating in the area where you might have been? Did they put any names to you?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Approximately how long did this meeting with them in Pristina at the State Security Centre last?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, about an hour, an hour and a half, not more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And were you treated well during it by them?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They just put questions to us and we gave answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Were you treated well? Did they threaten you or anything of that kind?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they did not threaten me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Other than this meeting on this day that lasted about one hour, did you have any other interviews or meetings with Serbian police or army or anyone from the state security apparatus as far as you remember?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't have any.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Very well. I only want to ask you two things about what took place in the seven or eight days that you were held. First of all, Mr. Bakrac, could you give us an estimation of the number of soldiers, guards, whatever you'd like to call them, that you -- that were at this place while you were held there? Can you give us any idea of how many?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you consider everybody to be the soldiers, I'm sure that there were seven or six who I know, who I used to meet. I cannot say anything about those that I didn't see.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Of course you can't, sir. One of the reasons I ask you is because we're going to be hearing from your son, and in his statement to the ICTY he estimates --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we're going to hear from him - I apologise for rising - but I'm not sure it's appropriate to go down this path.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's cross-examination, Mr. Black. It can be put to him unless somebody else has said something different.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I apologise for rising.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your son estimated in a statement he made that there were some at least 50 soldiers at this place. Now, you can only speak from your experience, Mr. Bakrac, of course. But what do you say about that estimate, 50?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that would be a bit of an exaggeration because he probably included all the soldiers. I referred only to those who I knew. I cannot say anything about those I didn't know and I didn't see. I know of the six or seven who were milling about all the time. I don't know about the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Could one of the difficulties, Mr. Bakrac, have been that some -- some of these soldiers, if that's what they were, were masked? Did some wear masks?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did aware masks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I'm going to show you, sir, a photograph, and I want you to be clear. I'm not suggesting that there is anyone in this photograph who is or even might have been at this place. That's not the purpose of showing it to you. It's for another purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: It's the same photograph, Your Honours, that I showed the previous witness. It comes from Prosecution Exhibit P18, and I wonder whether it could be put on the Sanction for us all to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, that is a group of men and women. I want to ask you two questions, really, about this photograph. The first is this: Looking at those uniforms, did you see anyone wearing uniforms similar to the black uniforms that we see on these people in this photograph when you were at the place you were held?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, one night when they came to watch television, a few of them that I saw for the first time then.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: The gentleman who is sitting with his right-hand to his chin next to a woman is in a different kind of uniform, I'll describe it as camouflage. Was that a uniform that you saw while you were there as well?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw camouflage uniforms, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: On the arm of the woman to the extreme right of the photograph is an armband. We can't see all of it, but I can I think with confidence suggest to you that that armband has the letters "PU" on it. Have you ever seen such an armband being worn before, Mr. Bakrac, by anyone?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: That's the general question, now the specific. Did you ever see anyone at the place where you were held for seven days wearing an armband with the letters "PU" on it?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And for the sake of completeness, and the Chamber will understand why I ask the question, did you ever see anyone with a cap badge with the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. letters "PU" on it while you were held at the place for seven or eight days?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. But I never looked at these people directly because I was afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, we understand that answer entirely, Mr. Bakrac, of course. But may I suggest s sir, and it's my last question on the photograph, that it would have been difficult to look at anyone without noticing a mask? Now -- at least masks like these. If you look in this photograph if you look carefully, sir, you'll see five people, three standing and two sitting who appear to have masks on. First of all, would you agree with me that there are five?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see three and one down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes. Next to the lady who's smiling --

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not five.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, maybe the quality of your screen -- perhaps it doesn't much matter. Focus if you would, please, on the three people who are standing, all right? Those masks that they're wearing, do you first of all agree with me that two of them seem to be of a similar style to each other and slightly different to the one in the middle? Do you agree with that, first of all?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Good. Now, looking at the people who are standing, first of all, did you ever see anyone at the place you were held wearing a mask like that?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one night when they came to the basement to get Genov.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: On any other occasion, apart from that one?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't have occasion to see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Now, looking at the person in the middle of the three masked individuals with the slightly different style of mask revealing, you may agree, Mr. Genov [sic], rather more of the eyes of the wearer, did you ever see anyone wearing a mask like that while you were being held?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all I ask you about the photograph. Mr. Bakrac, do you remember meeting with a Mr. Vasil Dimitrov after you had been released?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Right now the name doesn't mean anything to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, let me help you. At the Yugoslav Red Cross office in Pristina, we will hear from Vasil Dimitrov who I apprehend will tell us that he met with you and Ivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise for rising again, but if he's going to ask the witness to comment on another witness's testimony or another witness's statement, I don't think that's appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: On what basis do you put that submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: He can put these facts to him but he doesn't need to mention the names of these particular witnesses. That would be my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What's your submission, Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, I'm just trying to make life easier for Mr. Black's own witness, that's all. There can't possibly, in my submission, be anything inappropriate, still less improper, than asking him about a meeting he had with a man who has made a statement who is going to come and give evidence, rather like his son Ivan, about numbers of soldiers. I just simply want to ask him, to help him, whether he remembers meeting with this man. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm certainly in favour of anything that helps the witness, but my understanding of the practice here is that of course you can mention someone's name but then you don't need to point out the fact that they're going to be a witness. Otherwise -- if you're going to talk about things that are going to come up later in testimony you can give those facts, but you don't need to specify what witness it's coming from or that it will be testimony in the case. That's my submission, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't see the problem in that information being provided, and I'm not aware of there being a practice, certainly not a rule to the contrary. The fact that they will be a witness may be superfluous to the question, but otherwise --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: It probably is, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: It doesn't give what he says in his statement any more force or weight. It's just to help the witness, explain who the person is, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, I'm sorry. We have, as it were, been talking over you. I apologise. Do you remember him now, this man you met in Pristina, Yugoslav Red Cross office? His name was Dimitrov. Do you remember him?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I explain something?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met quite a few people there that day at the Red Cross, but I wouldn't know their names, I wouldn't know what I talked about, I don't know who I talked to. I really don't remember any of that. I know that I did talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, if I may say so, sir, it's a fair answer. I just wanted to ask you this: It seems that in those first few days of your release, as you just said, you spoke to a number of people in a number of places. I just want to see if I can understand and get a sense of the order in which these meetings and conversations were happening. Please take it from me you met this man Dimitrov in this place in Pristina. Now, he's from the Red Cross. Do you think that might have been before or after your meeting with state security, or the same day? Or can't you say?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I first went to the police on that day, and then to the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Right. Well, that's very helpful. Thank you. Again, I'm not going to ask you the detail of your meeting with Mr. Dimitrov, whose name you can't even remember, but again do you recollect now with the Red Cross giving them quite a bit of detail of what had been happening to you and your son Ivan? Do you remember doing that much, at least?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we talked about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Again, did the person at the Red Cross you were speaking to seem to know anything at all about the place you were talking to him about? Did he give any indication to you at all that he'd heard about this before?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, but I don't think that I was given any indication.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: As you sat there with him and as you had sat there with the police, Mr. Bakrac, it was your firm belief, was it, that Stamen Genov was dead?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: After this meeting with the Red Cross, did you ever meet with them again? Did you ever meet that same man again or speak to him again after this meeting as the weeks and months went by?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember having talked to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Did anyone ever tell you that there was some indication that Genov might not be dead, that Genov might in fact be alive? Have you heard that before from anywhere, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You mean to tell us, sir, the first time you've heard that said is when I just said it to you?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that would be right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: That's all I ask you, sir. Thank you for your patience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions. I'm grateful the witness has attended court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I do have, but a number. However, before I start my questioning of the witness, I'm wondering whether I could do two things, with the Court's indulgence and with the Office of the Prosecutor's agreement. Yesterday a matter had occurred with regard to Witness L-04 and I have given to each of Your Honours an agreed fact, which I would like to read into the record and it was hoped that I could do that before I start questioning Mr. Bakrac. The second matter that I would like to engage in is entering another agreed fact into the record that is directly related to Mr. Bakrac's testimony and will, as a result of this agreed fact, greatly shorten his testimony. So with the Court's indulgence I would like to do that at this time, if that's permissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is there any difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
